hydrology.why: With a constant flux through the unsaturated zone, Richards's equation fixes the suction at every height: capillary rise for evaporation, a unit-gradient tail for infiltration.
hydrology.limit: Richards (1931) steady equation ``flux = -K(psi) (dpsi/dz + 1)`` with Gardner's (1958) conductivity; an upward flux can only be sustained below ``np.log(1 + saturated_conductivity / flux) / sorptive_number``.

hydrology.name: nash_unit_hydrograph
hydrology.title: Instantaneous unit hydrograph of a cascade of linear reservoirs

params.name: time
params.unit: s, since the instant of excess rainfall

params.name: storage_constant
params.unit: s, Nash's k of each reservoir

hydrology.why: A catchment that drains like a chain of equal linear reservoirs turns an instant of rain into a skewed, gamma-shaped pulse of river flow.
hydrology.limit: Nash (1957), a gamma density with mean lag ``reservoirs * storage_constant``; a smooth synthetic shape for Sherman's unit hydrograph, linear and time-invariant.

hydrology.name: unit_hydrograph_convolution
hydrology.title: Storm hydrograph from excess rainfall and a unit hydrograph

params.name: excess_rainfall
params.unit: m, excess (effective) rainfall depth in each interval

params.name: unit_hydrograph
params.unit: m^3/s per metre of excess rainfall, ordinates at the same interval

hydrology.why: If a catchment responds linearly, the flood from any storm is the sum of unit-hydrograph responses to its successive bursts of excess rainfall, each shifted and scaled.
hydrology.limit: Sherman (1932): linear superposition and time invariance; baseflow and losses are removed beforehand.

hydrology.name: horton_infiltration_rate
hydrology.title: Horton's infiltration capacity during a storm

params.name: time
params.unit: s, since the soil began to infiltrate at capacity

hydrology.why: Infiltration capacity falls from a high initial value to a steady one as the soil wets, and rain beyond it runs off over the surface.
hydrology.limit: Horton (1933, 1940), an empirical law for rain at or above capacity throughout.

hydrology.name: horton_cumulative_infiltration
hydrology.title: Depth infiltrated under Horton's law
hydrology.expr: final_rate * time + (initial_rate - final_rate) * (1 - np.exp(-decay_constant * time)) / decay_constant
hydrology.why: The time integral of Horton's capacity is the water the soil can take up before the steady rate dominates.
hydrology.limit: Horton (1933, 1940), with rain at or above capacity from time zero.

hydrology.name: well_function
hydrology.title: Theis well function W(u)
hydrology.why: The drawdown around a pumped well is a universal curve of one combination of distance, time and aquifer properties.
hydrology.limit: The exponential integral E1, ``-0.5772 - ln(u) + u - ...`` for small u.

hydrology.name: theis_drawdown
hydrology.title: Drawdown around a well pumping a confined aquifer
hydrology.expr: pumping_rate / (4 * np.pi * transmissivity) * scipy.special.exp1(radius**2 * storativity / (4 * transmissivity * time))
hydrology.why: Theis took the heat-conduction solution for a line sink and found that the cone of depression keeps growing as the well draws water from storage.
hydrology.limit: Theis (1935): constant rate, a fully penetrating well of negligible radius in an infinite, homogeneous, isotropic confined aquifer with water released instantly from storage.

hydrology.name: muskingum_coefficients
hydrology.title: Muskingum routing coefficients

params.name: storage_constant
params.unit: s, Muskingum K, about the travel time through the reach

hydrology.expr: [time_step - 2 K X, time_step + 2 K X, 2 K (1 - X) - time_step] / (2 K (1 - X) + time_step)
hydrology.why: Storage in a river reach is a weighted mix of inflow and outflow, which makes the outflow a fixed linear combination of the latest flows.
hydrology.limit: McCarthy (1938), storage ``K (X I + (1 - X) O)``; all coefficients are nonnegative when ``2 K X <= time_step <= 2 K (1 - X)``.

hydrology.name: muskingum_routing
hydrology.title: Outflow hydrograph of a river reach by the Muskingum method
hydrology.why: Routing a flood through a reach delays and flattens its peak, the effect forecasters need downstream.
hydrology.limit: McCarthy (1938): ``O[j+1] = C0 I[j+1] + C1 I[j] + C2 O[j]``; choose the time step so that no coefficient is negative.

hydrology.name: stream_number
hydrology.title: Number of streams of a given order in a drainage network
hydrology.why: Horton found that stream counts fall geometrically with order, so a whole river network is summarized by one bifurcation ratio.
hydrology.limit: Horton's law of stream numbers (1945), an empirical average; Strahler's (1952) ordering is the usual convention.

hydrology.name: stream_length
hydrology.title: Mean length of the streams of a given order

params.name: first_order_length
params.unit: m, mean length of first-order streams

hydrology.why: Streams grow longer geometrically with order, Horton's companion to his law of stream numbers.
hydrology.limit: Horton's law of stream lengths (1945), an empirical average over a network.

hydrology.name: cooper_jacob_drawdown
hydrology.title: Cooper and Jacob's late-time approximation to the Theis drawdown
hydrology.expr: pumping_rate / (4 * np.pi * transmissivity) * (-np.euler_gamma - np.log(radius**2 * storativity / (4 * transmissivity * time)))
hydrology.why: Late in a pumping test the drawdown grows linearly with the logarithm of time, so a straight line on a semilog plot gives the aquifer properties.
hydrology.limit: Cooper and Jacob (1946): the first two terms of the Theis series, within 1% for ``u < 0.01`` and meaningless (it goes negative) for u above about 0.56.

hydrology.name: cooper_jacob_transmissivity
hydrology.title: Transmissivity from the slope of a Cooper-Jacob straight line

params.name: drawdown_per_log_cycle
params.unit: m, drawdown increase per factor of ten in time

hydrology.why: The drawdown gained per tenfold increase in time depends only on the pumping rate and the transmissivity.
hydrology.limit: Cooper and Jacob (1946), from late-time data where ``u < 0.01``; the storativity follows from the zero-drawdown intercept ``t0`` as ``2.25 * transmissivity * t0 / radius**2``.

hydrology.name: saturation_slope
hydrology.title: Slope of the saturation vapour-pressure curve
hydrology.why: The steepness of the Clausius-Clapeyron curve converts a surface-to-air temperature difference into a vapour-pressure difference.
hydrology.limit: Derivative of :func:`earthsciencekit.atmosphere.saturation_vapor_pressure` (constant latent heat 2.5e6 J/kg).

hydrology.name: psychrometric_constant
hydrology.title: Psychrometric constant
hydrology.why: It converts a temperature difference into the vapour-pressure difference that carries the same energy, as sensible rather than latent heat.
hydrology.limit: Dry-air heat capacity and constant latent heat; equal transfer coefficients for heat and vapour.

hydrology.name: penman_evaporation
hydrology.title: Penman's combination equation for open-water evaporation

params.name: net_radiation
params.unit: W/m^2, net radiation minus heat stored below the surface

params.name: aerodynamic_evaporation
params.unit: kg/(m^2 s), Dalton's evaporation evaluated with the air temperature, ``f(u) (e_s(T_air) - e_air)``

hydrology.why: Penman eliminated the unknown surface temperature by combining the energy balance with Dalton's law, so evaporation follows from routine weather measurements.
hydrology.limit: Penman (1948): the saturation curve is linearized between air and surface temperature, and heat and vapour share one transfer coefficient; a saturated surface (open water or wet grass).

hydrology.name: aerodynamic_resistance
hydrology.title: Aerodynamic resistance to vapour transfer above a canopy

params.name: displacement_height
params.unit: m, zero-plane displacement (about two thirds of the canopy height)

params.name: vapor_roughness
params.unit: m, often a tenth of the momentum roughness

hydrology.expr: np.log((measurement_height - displacement_height) / momentum_roughness) * np.log((measurement_height - displacement_height) / vapor_roughness) / (VON_KARMAN**2 * wind_speed)
hydrology.why: Turbulence in the logarithmic wind profile carries vapour away from the canopy, faster in stronger wind over rougher surfaces.
hydrology.limit: Neutral stability; the measurement height above the displacement height must exceed both roughness lengths. For FAO grass (0.12 m) at 2 m it is about ``208 / wind_speed``.

hydrology.name: bulk_surface_resistance
hydrology.title: Bulk surface (canopy) resistance from the leaf stomatal resistance

params.name: stomatal_resistance
params.unit: s/m, of a single well-illuminated leaf (about 100)

params.name: active_leaf_area_index
params.unit: 1, sunlit leaf area per ground area (about half the leaf area index)

hydrology.why: The stomata of all leaves act as resistances in parallel, so a dense canopy offers less resistance than a single leaf.
hydrology.limit: Monteith (1965) big-leaf canopy with parallel leaves; FAO grass has about 70 s/m.

hydrology.name: penman_monteith_evaporation
hydrology.title: Penman-Monteith evaporation from a vegetated surface

params.name: available_energy
params.unit: W/m^2, net radiation minus ground heat flux

hydrology.expr: (Delta * available_energy + air_density * CP_DRY_AIR * vapor_pressure_deficit / aerodynamic_resistance) / (LATENT_HEAT_VAPORIZATION * (Delta + gamma * (1 + surface_resistance / aerodynamic_resistance)))
hydrology.why: Monteith added the resistance of the stomata to Penman's equation, so the same formula covers open water, wet leaves and transpiring crops.
hydrology.limit: Monteith (1965): a big-leaf canopy at one temperature, neutral stability; zero surface resistance recovers Penman with ``aerodynamic_evaporation = air_density * CP_DRY_AIR * vapor_pressure_deficit / (psychrometric_constant * LATENT_HEAT_VAPORIZATION * aerodynamic_resistance)``.

hydrology.name: topographic_index
hydrology.title: TOPMODEL topographic wetness index

params.name: specific_area
params.unit: m, upslope area drained per unit contour width

hydrology.why: Ground that drains a large upslope area through a gentle slope is the first to saturate, so one number from the topography maps where runoff starts.
hydrology.limit: Beven and Kirkby (1979): steady recharge, a water table parallel to the surface and transmissivity falling exponentially with deficit.

hydrology.name: topmodel_deficit
hydrology.title: Local storage deficit of TOPMODEL from the catchment mean

params.name: scaling_depth
params.unit: m, TOPMODEL's m, the deficit that reduces transmissivity by a factor e

hydrology.why: Each point's deficit departs from the catchment mean in proportion to how much wetter its topographic index is than average, so one state variable maps the saturated area.
hydrology.limit: Beven and Kirkby (1979) with uniform transmissivity at saturation and quasi-steady drainage.

hydrology.name: topmodel_baseflow
hydrology.title: TOPMODEL subsurface drainage from the catchment-mean deficit

params.name: saturated_transmissivity
params.unit: m^2/s, transmissivity when the soil is saturated to the surface

params.name: mean_index
params.unit: 1, catchment mean of ``ln(a / tan(beta))`` with a in metres

hydrology.why: Baseflow falls exponentially as the catchment dries, the recession behaviour TOPMODEL is built on.
hydrology.limit: Beven and Kirkby (1979): exponential transmissivity profile, water table parallel to the surface.

hydrology.name: exponential_water_content
hydrology.title: Volumetric water content of an exponential (Gardner-Russo) soil
hydrology.why: Water drains from the largest pores first, so the water content falls with suction; with the same exponent as Gardner's conductivity, Richards's equation becomes linear.
hydrology.limit: Russo (1988) retention paired with Gardner's (1958) conductivity; no air-entry value or hysteresis.

hydrology.name: kinematic_wave_celerity
hydrology.title: Speed at which a flood wave travels down a channel
hydrology.why: A flood crest moves faster than the water in it, because deeper water flows faster: by 5/3 for Manning's law in a wide channel.
hydrology.limit: Lighthill and Whitham (1955): single-valued rating, friction balancing the bed slope; no attenuation.

hydrology.name: degree_day_melt
hydrology.title: Snowmelt rate from the air temperature by the degree-day method
hydrology.why: Air temperature alone, the one weather variable measured almost everywhere, predicts melt well over days because it tracks most of the energy that reaches the snow.
hydrology.limit: Finsterwalder and Schunk (1887): periods of a day or longer with snow present; the factor varies with season, site and snow age.

hydrology.name: snowpack_water_equivalent
hydrology.title: Snow water equivalent and water released by a degree-day snowpack

params.name: precipitation
params.unit: m of water equivalent per step

hydrology.expr: melt = min(swe + snowfall, degree_day_factor * max(T - T0, 0) * time_step); swe = swe + snowfall - melt
hydrology.why: Snow stores winter precipitation and releases it as melt in spring, the delay that shapes the hydrograph of every mountain river.
hydrology.limit: Single-layer degree-day snowpack starting bare; one threshold for snowfall and melt; no refreezing, liquid storage or sublimation; last axis holds SWE and released water.
hydrology.extra: temperature and precipitation are matching vectors

glaciology.name: ela_shift
glaciology.title: Shift of the equilibrium-line altitude with a change of climate

params.name: temperature_change
params.unit: K, change of summer air temperature at fixed altitude

params.name: lapse_rate
params.unit: K/m, decrease of temperature with height

glaciology.why: A colder climate brings the snow line down the mountains, and the glaciers grow to meet it.
glaciology.limit: Temperature alone controls ablation and the lapse rate is uniform; changes of snowfall also move the line.

glaciology.name: driving_stress
glaciology.title: Gravitational driving stress of a glacier or ice sheet
glaciology.why: The weight of the ice resolved down the surface slope is what the bed and the ice must resist.
glaciology.limit: Shallow-ice balance: horizontal scales much larger than the thickness, small slopes, longitudinal stresses neglected.

glaciology.name: viscous_slab_velocity
glaciology.title: Velocity in a Newtonian viscous slab flowing down a slope
glaciology.expr: density * gravity * surface_slope * (2 * thickness * height - height**2) / (2 * viscosity)
glaciology.why: Forbes argued that a glacier flows like a very viscous fluid, fastest at the surface and slowest against its bed.
glaciology.limit: Forbes (1843): a wide parallel-sided slab with a linear viscosity, no sliding and small slope.

glaciology.name: isostatic_depression
glaciology.title: Equilibrium depression of the land under an ice sheet
glaciology.why: The mantle under a wide ice sheet gives way until the displaced rock weighs as much as the ice, about a third of its thickness.
glaciology.limit: Jamieson (1865): local isostasy for a load much wider than the flexural wavelength of the lithosphere.

glaciology.name: stefan_ice_thickness
glaciology.title: Stefan's thickness of ice grown by conduction through itself

params.name: freezing_degree_time
params.unit: K s, time integral of the freezing temperature minus the surface temperature

glaciology.why: The latent heat released at the base of the ice must be conducted up through ice already formed, so the thickness grows only as the square root of the accumulated cold.
glaciology.limit: Stefan (1891): ice free of snow, with its surface at the air temperature, a linear temperature profile, no ocean heat flux and no initial ice; it overestimates growth under snow.

glaciology.name: stefan_growth_rate
glaciology.title: Basal growth rate of ice in Stefan's problem

params.name: temperature_difference
params.unit: K, freezing temperature minus surface temperature

glaciology.why: Thin ice grows fast and thick ice slowly, because the conductive heat flux falls with thickness.
glaciology.limit: Stefan (1891), quasi-steady conduction with no ocean heat flux.

glaciology.name: sea_ice_freeboard
glaciology.title: Height of floating snow-free ice above the waterline
glaciology.why: Satellite altimeters measure the freeboard, and Archimedes' principle turns it into a thickness about ten times larger.
glaciology.limit: Hydrostatic equilibrium of a uniform floe without snow load.

glaciology.name: viscous_relaxation_time
glaciology.title: Relaxation time of a surface depression on a viscous half-space
glaciology.why: A broad depression in a viscous mantle recovers faster than a narrow one, so the timing of rebound measures the viscosity.
glaciology.limit: Haskell (1935): a uniform Newtonian half-space without an elastic lithosphere, which slows the shortest wavelengths.

glaciology.name: haskell_viscosity
glaciology.title: Mantle viscosity inferred from a rebound relaxation time
glaciology.why: Haskell turned the uplift of Fennoscandia into the first estimate of the viscosity of the mantle, about 1e21 Pa s.
glaciology.limit: Haskell (1935), the inverse of viscous_relaxation_time for a uniform half-space.

glaciology.name: remaining_depression
glaciology.title: Depression still to be recovered after the ice has gone

params.name: time
params.unit: s, since the ice was removed

glaciology.why: After the ice sheet melts the land rises exponentially, and the uplift still to come falls by e every relaxation time.
glaciology.limit: Haskell (1935): one wavelength on a viscous half-space, with the load removed at once.

glaciology.name: rebound_uplift_rate
glaciology.title: Rate of postglacial uplift

params.name: time
params.unit: s, since the ice was removed

glaciology.why: The land rises fastest just after deglaciation; Fennoscandia still rises by up to 9 mm a year.
glaciology.limit: Haskell (1935), the time derivative of remaining_depression.

glaciology.name: nye_plastic_profile
glaciology.title: Surface height of a perfectly plastic ice sheet on a flat bed
glaciology.why: If ice yields at a fixed stress, the ice sheet takes a parabolic profile whose height depends only on the distance from its margin.
glaciology.limit: Nye (1951): a horizontal bed, basal shear stress everywhere equal to the yield stress and no isostatic depression.

glaciology.name: glen_strain_rate
glaciology.title: Glen's flow law: strain rate of polycrystalline ice
glaciology.why: Glen's creep tests showed that ice deforms at a rate proportional to roughly the cube of the stress, so it is far from a Newtonian fluid.
glaciology.limit: Glen (1955): secondary creep of isotropic ice at stresses of about 0.05-1 MPa.

glaciology.name: glen_stress
glaciology.title: Stress needed to deform ice at a given strain rate
glaciology.why: Inverting Glen's law turns a measured stretching rate into the stress that drives it.
glaciology.limit: Glen (1955), inverted; secondary creep of isotropic ice.

glaciology.name: glen_rate_factor
glaciology.title: Arrhenius temperature dependence of Glen's rate factor

params.name: temperature
params.unit: K, ice temperature (relative to the pressure-melting point)

glaciology.why: Ice near its melting point is softer by more than an order of magnitude than ice at -30 degC.
glaciology.limit: An Arrhenius law with one activation energy, about 60 kJ/mol below -10 degC and 115 kJ/mol above (Cuffey and Paterson 2010), for temperate-ice water contents neglected.

glaciology.name: effective_viscosity
glaciology.title: Effective viscosity of ice under Glen's law
glaciology.why: Ice under a large stress behaves as a much less viscous fluid than ice under a small one.
glaciology.limit: Glen (1955), written as a stress-dependent Newtonian viscosity; with n = 1 it is the viscosity 1 / (2 A).

glaciology.name: glen_velocity_profile
glaciology.title: Deformation velocity through a glacier obeying Glen's law
glaciology.why: Most of the shearing in a frozen-bed glacier happens near the bed, so the velocity is nearly uniform in its upper half.
glaciology.limit: Nye (1952) laminar flow with Glen (1955) rheology: a wide slab, uniform rate factor and no sliding.

glaciology.name: glen_surface_velocity
glaciology.title: Surface velocity of a glacier deforming by Glen's law
glaciology.why: The surface speed rises with the fourth power of thickness and the cube of slope, which is why thick glaciers flow so much faster than thin ones.
glaciology.limit: Nye (1952) laminar flow with Glen (1955) rheology, no sliding.

glaciology.name: nye_crevasse_depth
glaciology.title: Depth of a dry crevasse in stretching ice
glaciology.why: A crevasse can only stay open where the tensile stress from stretching exceeds the closing pressure of the ice, which caps dry crevasses at a few tens of metres.
glaciology.limit: Nye (1955): a field of closely spaced crevasses in uniform ice of density independent of depth; fracture toughness is neglected.

glaciology.name: water_filled_crevasse_depth
glaciology.title: Depth of a crevasse partly filled with meltwater

params.name: water_depth
params.unit: m, height of water standing in the crevasse

glaciology.expr: 2 * (strain_rate / rate_factor) ** (1 / exponent) / (ice_density * gravity) + water_density / ice_density * water_depth
glaciology.why: Water is denser than ice, so a water-filled crevasse is pushed deeper than a dry one and can cut through a whole ice shelf.
glaciology.limit: Nye (1955) with the water pressure added (Benn et al. 2007); the result is meaningful only while it is less than the ice thickness and at least the water depth.

glaciology.name: weertman_sliding_velocity
glaciology.title: Weertman's sliding velocity of temperate ice over a rough bed
glaciology.why: Ice gets past bed obstacles by regelation around small ones and enhanced creep around large ones, which makes the sliding speed a power of the basal stress.
glaciology.limit: Weertman (1957): a bed at the melting point, free of cavities and sediment; the coefficient lumps the bed roughness.

glaciology.name: linear_mass_balance
glaciology.title: Surface mass balance rising linearly with altitude

params.name: balance_gradient
params.unit: 1/s, metres of ice per second per metre of altitude

glaciology.why: A glacier gains mass above its equilibrium line and loses it below, at a rate that grows steadily with the distance from the line.
glaciology.limit: Meier (1962): the balance gradient is about 0.003-0.01 m of water per year per metre on mid-latitude glaciers; real profiles flatten at high altitude.

glaciology.name: accumulation_area_ratio
glaciology.title: Fraction of a glacier's area above its equilibrium line
glaciology.why: A glacier in balance with its climate keeps a characteristic share of its area in the accumulation zone, about 0.6.
glaciology.limit: Meier (1962); the steady-state ratio depends on the glacier's hypsometry and is not universal.

glaciology.name: dansgaard_delta
glaciology.title: Oxygen-isotope ratio of precipitation from the air temperature

params.name: temperature
params.unit: K, mean annual surface air temperature

params.name: offset
params.unit: permil, the delta at 0 degC, about -13.6

glaciology.why: Air loses its heavy isotopes first as it cools and rains out, so the snow at colder sites is lighter.
glaciology.limit: Dansgaard (1964): a spatial relation for mid- and high-latitude coastal and polar stations; the temporal slope at one site can differ.

glaciology.name: dansgaard_temperature
glaciology.title: Air temperature recorded by the oxygen-isotope ratio of snow
glaciology.why: Inverting Dansgaard's relation turns the isotope profile of an ice core into a temperature history.
glaciology.limit: Dansgaard (1964), inverted; the spatial slope is an approximation of the temporal one.

glaciology.name: nye_age
glaciology.title: Age of ice at depth when layers thin uniformly

params.name: depth
params.unit: m, of ice equivalent below the surface
params.kind: between 0 and thickness, exclusive of thickness

glaciology.why: In a steady ice sheet each layer thins in proportion to its height above the bed, so age grows logarithmically with depth.
glaciology.limit: Nye (1963): a steady divide with uniform vertical strain rate, no basal melting or sliding; the age diverges at the bed.

glaciology.name: dansgaard_johnsen_downward_velocity
glaciology.title: Vertical ice velocity in the Dansgaard-Johnsen flow model

params.name: depth
params.unit: m of ice below the surface

glaciology.expr: np.where(z >= h, accumulation * (2 * z - h) / (2 * thickness - h), accumulation * z**2 / (h * (2 * thickness - h)))
glaciology.why: Ice frozen to its bed shears only near the bottom, so the vertical velocity falls linearly down to a kink and then quadratically to zero at the bed.
glaciology.limit: Dansgaard and Johnsen (1969): steady state, constant horizontal strain rate above the kink and a linear decrease below it, no basal melting. Below, z = thickness - depth and h = kink_height.

glaciology.name: dansgaard_johnsen_age
glaciology.title: Age of ice at depth in the Dansgaard-Johnsen flow model

params.name: depth
params.unit: m of ice below the surface
params.kind: between 0 and thickness, exclusive of thickness

glaciology.expr: s / (2 * a) * np.log(s / (2 * np.maximum(z, h) - h)) + h * s / a * (1 / np.minimum(z, h) - 1 / h)
glaciology.why: The first time scale for a deep ice core, Camp Century, integrated the thinning of annual layers down to the kink and below it.
glaciology.limit: Dansgaard and Johnsen (1969), the integral of the reciprocal of dansgaard_johnsen_downward_velocity; it tends to nye_age as the kink height goes to zero. Below, z = thickness - depth, h = kink_height, a = accumulation and s = 2 * thickness - h.

glaciology.name: flotation_thickness
glaciology.title: Thickness at which ice resting on a submarine bed begins to float
glaciology.why: The grounding line of a marine ice sheet sits where the ice is just thin enough to float, so its thickness is set by the water depth alone.
glaciology.limit: Archimedes' principle for an ice column of uniform density.

glaciology.name: ice_shelf_strain_rate
glaciology.title: Spreading rate of a freely floating ice shelf
glaciology.expr: rate_factor * (ice_density * gravity * thickness * (1 - ice_density / water_density) / 4) ** exponent
glaciology.why: A floating shelf spreads under the difference between its weight and the water pressure, faster the thicker it is.
glaciology.limit: Weertman (1957) for an unconfined shelf spreading in one direction, without buttressing or side drag.

glaciology.name: shallow_ice_flux
glaciology.title: Ice flux per unit width in the shallow-ice approximation
glaciology.why: In a thin ice sheet the flux at each point depends only on the local thickness and surface slope.
glaciology.limit: Hutter (1983) and Mahaffy (1976): Glen ice frozen to its bed, aspect ratio small, uniform rate factor.

glaciology.name: shallow_ice_diffusivity
glaciology.title: Nonlinear diffusivity of the shallow-ice equation
glaciology.why: The shallow-ice approximation makes the ice thickness obey a diffusion equation whose diffusivity grows steeply with thickness and slope.
glaciology.limit: Mahaffy (1976): the shallow-ice approximation for Glen ice frozen to its bed. Below, A = rate_factor, n = exponent.

glaciology.name: vialov_dome_height
glaciology.title: Central height of a steady shallow-ice sheet
glaciology.expr: (2 * ((n + 2) * accumulation / (2 * A * (density * gravity) ** n)) ** (1 / n)) ** (n / (2 * n + 2)) * np.sqrt(half_width)
glaciology.why: An ice sheet in balance with a uniform snowfall has a dome height that grows only as the square root of its width.
glaciology.limit: Vialov (1958): a flat bed, uniform accumulation up to a fixed margin, shallow-ice flow without sliding. Below, A = rate_factor, n = exponent.

glaciology.name: vialov_profile
glaciology.title: Surface profile of a steady shallow-ice sheet
glaciology.why: Glen's law flattens the dome and steepens the margin of a steady ice sheet compared with Nye's parabola.
glaciology.limit: Vialov (1958), see vialov_dome_height; the shallow-ice approximation fails within a few thicknesses of the divide and the margin.

glaciology.name: glacier_response_time
glaciology.title: Volume response time of a glacier to a change of climate

params.name: terminus_ablation
params.unit: m/s of ice, ablation rate at the terminus as a positive magnitude

glaciology.why: A glacier adjusts to a new climate in about the time its terminus ablation takes to remove its own thickness.
glaciology.limit: Johannesson, Raymond and Waddington (1989): a linear response of volume; decades for valley glaciers, millennia for ice sheets.

glaciology.name: gas_age_difference
glaciology.title: Age difference between the ice and the air trapped in it

params.name: mean_firn_density
params.unit: kg/m^3, mean density of the firn above it

glaciology.why: Air stays connected to the atmosphere through the porous firn until the bubbles close, so the gas in a core is younger than the ice around it.
glaciology.limit: Schwander and Stauffer (1984), as used for Vostok by Barnola et al. (1987): steady firn densification with no thinning above close-off; diffusion through the open pores, which makes the gas slightly older, is neglected.

glaciology.name: schoof_grounding_line_flux
glaciology.title: Schoof's ice flux across the grounding line of a marine ice sheet

params.name: grounding_thickness
params.unit: m, the flotation thickness at the grounding line

params.name: friction_coefficient
params.unit: Pa (s/m)^m, the C of a basal stress C u^m

params.name: friction_exponent
params.unit: 1, the m of a basal stress C u^m, such as 1/3

glaciology.why: The flux out of a marine ice sheet is set by the ice thickness at its grounding line, and rises so steeply with it that a grounding line on a bed deepening inland cannot be steady.
glaciology.limit: Schoof (2007): a flowline with a power-law sliding bed, an unbuttressed shelf and a boundary layer at the grounding line; steady states are stable only where the bed rises inland. Below, A = rate_factor, n = exponent, C = friction_coefficient, m = friction_exponent, rho_i = ice_density, rho_w = water_density, h = grounding_thickness.

glaciology.name: herron_langway_density
glaciology.title: Density of steady-state firn at a depth, by the Herron-Langway model
glaciology.expr: ICE_DENSITY / (1 + np.exp(-x)), x = logit(surface_density) + rho_i k0 * depth above the critical depth and logit(550) + rho_i k1 / A**0.5 * (depth - critical_depth) below it
glaciology.why: Snow compacts under its own weight into firn and then into ice, so the density profile sets how deep air stays open to the atmosphere and how much the ice is younger than the snow it buries.
glaciology.limit: Herron and Langway (1980): empirical steady-state dry firn, two stages split at 550 kg/m^3, fitted with densities in Mg/m^3 and accumulation in m/yr of water; no melt, layering or transient climate.
glaciology.extra: logit(rho) = ln(rho / (ICE_DENSITY - rho)); k0 = 11 exp(-10160 / (R T)), k1 = 575 exp(-21400 / (R T)); A = accumulation * SECONDS_PER_YEAR * ICE_DENSITY / 1000; surface_density < 550

glaciology.name: herron_langway_depth
glaciology.title: Depth at which steady-state Herron-Langway firn reaches a density
glaciology.expr: (logit(density) - logit(surface_density)) / (rho_i k0) up to 550 kg/m^3, then critical_depth + (logit(density) - logit(550)) * A**0.5 / (rho_i k1)
glaciology.why: The depth of the pore close-off density, about 830 kg/m^3, is where the air in the firn is sealed into bubbles.
glaciology.limit: Herron and Langway (1980): empirical steady-state dry firn, two stages split at 550 kg/m^3, fitted with densities in Mg/m^3 and accumulation in m/yr of water; no melt, layering or transient climate.

glaciology.name: herron_langway_mean_density
glaciology.title: Mean density of steady-state Herron-Langway firn between the surface and a depth
glaciology.expr: (stage-one mass + stage-two mass) / depth, each stage of slope c holding ICE_DENSITY / c * ln((ICE_DENSITY - a) / (ICE_DENSITY - b)) between densities a and b
glaciology.why: The firn mass above the close-off depth, divided by the yearly accumulation, is the age of the ice there and so the ice-age minus gas-age difference.
glaciology.limit: Herron and Langway (1980): empirical steady-state dry firn, two stages split at 550 kg/m^3, fitted with densities in Mg/m^3 and accumulation in m/yr of water; no melt, layering or transient climate. Exact integral of herron_langway_density.

glaciology.name: expected_positive_degree_days
glaciology.title: Expected positive degree-days of a period with normally distributed temperature

params.name: mean_temperature
params.unit: K, mean air temperature of the period

params.name: standard_deviation
params.unit: K, of the daily temperature about that mean

glaciology.expr: duration * (s / np.sqrt(2 * np.pi) * np.exp(-c**2 / (2 * s**2)) + c / 2 * erfc(-c / (np.sqrt(2) * s))), c = mean_temperature - 273.15, s = standard_deviation
glaciology.why: A month whose mean is below freezing still has warm days that melt ice, so ice-sheet models count the positive part of a fluctuating temperature rather than of its mean.
glaciology.limit: Reeh (1991), closed form of Calov and Greve (2005): normal temperature about a fixed mean over the period; no day-to-day correlation or diurnal cycle.

glaciology.name: pdd_surface_melt
glaciology.title: Snow melt, ice melt and runoff of an ice-sheet surface from its positive degree-days
glaciology.expr: snow = np.minimum(snow_factor * pdd, snowfall); ice = ice_factor * np.maximum(pdd - snowfall / snow_factor, 0); runoff = snow + ice - np.minimum(refreezing_fraction * snowfall, snow + ice)
glaciology.why: The positive degree-days melt the year's snow first and then the darker ice beneath, and part of the meltwater refreezes in the cold snow, so runoff is less than melt.
glaciology.limit: Reeh (1991) with Braithwaite's factors: one annual layer; no rain, superimposed ice, albedo feedback or firn warming.
glaciology.extra: returns snow melt, ice melt and runoff on the last axis

geomorphology.name: stokes_settling_velocity
geomorphology.title: Stokes settling velocity of a small sphere

params.name: viscosity
params.unit: Pa s, dynamic viscosity of the fluid

geomorphology.why: Fine grains fall so slowly that viscosity alone resists them, which is why silt and clay stay in suspension.
geomorphology.limit: Stokes (1851): a smooth sphere at particle Reynolds number below about 1, roughly quartz finer than 0.1 mm in water.

geomorphology.name: ferguson_church_settling_velocity
geomorphology.title: Settling velocity of natural sand grains at any size
geomorphology.expr: R * gravity * diameter**2 / (18 * kinematic_viscosity + np.sqrt(0.75 * R * gravity * diameter**3)); R = sediment_density / fluid_density - 1
geomorphology.why: One formula spans viscous settling of silt and drag-dominated settling of gravel, joining Stokes's law to the turbulent limit.
geomorphology.limit: Ferguson and Church (2004) with C1 = 18 and C2 = 1 for natural grains; Stokes's law for fine grains and a constant drag coefficient for coarse ones; spheres need C2 = 0.4.

geomorphology.name: bed_shear_stress
geomorphology.title: Mean bed shear stress of steady uniform flow

params.name: hydraulic_radius
params.unit: m, the depth in a wide channel

geomorphology.why: The weight of the water resolved down the slope is balanced by friction on the bed, and that friction moves the sediment.
geomorphology.limit: The depth-slope product of steady uniform flow; bank friction and bedforms take part of it in real channels.

geomorphology.name: shear_velocity
geomorphology.title: Shear velocity of a flow over its bed
geomorphology.why: The bed shear stress expressed as a velocity sets the scale of near-bed turbulence.
geomorphology.limit: A definition; it applies to any turbulent boundary layer, in water or air.

geomorphology.name: shields_number
geomorphology.title: Shields number, the dimensionless bed shear stress
geomorphology.why: The ratio of the force that drives a grain to the submerged weight that holds it decides whether the bed moves.
geomorphology.limit: Shields (1936): uniform cohesionless grains on a nearly flat bed.

geomorphology.name: dimensionless_grain_size
geomorphology.title: Dimensionless grain size of a sediment in a fluid
geomorphology.why: One number combines grain size, density and viscosity, so that a single curve gives the threshold of motion for sand in water and in air.
geomorphology.limit: Soulsby and Whitehouse (1997); about 25 per millimetre of quartz in water at 20 degC.

geomorphology.name: critical_shields_number
geomorphology.title: Critical Shields number for the threshold of motion
geomorphology.why: The Shields curve falls from fine to medium sand and levels off for gravel, where a grain moves once the bed stress reaches about 5% of its submerged weight per unit area.
geomorphology.limit: Soulsby and Whitehouse (1997) fit to Shields's (1936) data, with the rise for fine grains; uniform cohesionless grains on a flat bed, with a scatter of about a factor of two.

geomorphology.name: keulegan_mean_velocity
geomorphology.title: Depth-averaged velocity of a rough turbulent channel flow

params.name: roughness_height
params.unit: m, Nikuradse's equivalent sand roughness, about 2.5 grain diameters on a flat bed

geomorphology.why: Integrating the logarithmic velocity profile over the depth turns a bed shear stress into the mean velocity a current meter would record.
geomorphology.limit: Keulegan (1938): fully rough flow in a wide channel with the von Karman constant 0.41; the depth should exceed the roughness several times.

geomorphology.name: rouse_number
geomorphology.title: Rouse number of suspended sediment
geomorphology.why: Settling pulls grains down while turbulence mixes them up; the ratio of the two sets how evenly they fill the flow.
geomorphology.limit: Rouse (1937), with the eddy diffusivity of sediment equal to that of momentum and the von Karman constant 0.41.

geomorphology.name: rouse_concentration
geomorphology.title: Rouse profile of suspended-sediment concentration

params.name: reference_height
params.unit: m, where the concentration is known

params.name: reference_concentration
params.unit: Any concentration unit, at the reference height

geomorphology.why: The balance of settling and turbulent mixing concentrates sediment near the bed, the more so the coarser the grains.
geomorphology.limit: Rouse (1937): steady uniform flow with a parabolic eddy diffusivity and dilute suspension; zero at the surface.

geomorphology.name: meyer_peter_muller_transport
geomorphology.title: Meyer-Peter and Müller dimensionless bedload transport rate
geomorphology.why: Bedload grows as the 3/2 power of the excess of the bed stress over its threshold, so a modest flood moves far more gravel than a long ordinary flow.
geomorphology.limit: Meyer-Peter and Müller (1948): flume data for well-sorted sand and gravel on a plane bed, with the skin friction part of the stress; Wong and Parker (2006) correct it to ``3.97 (theta - 0.0495)**1.5``.

geomorphology.name: bedload_flux
geomorphology.title: Volumetric bedload flux per unit width from the Einstein number
geomorphology.expr: transport_rate * np.sqrt((sediment_density / fluid_density - 1) * gravity * diameter) * diameter
geomorphology.why: The dimensionless transport rate scales back to a volume of grains crossing each metre of channel width per second.
geomorphology.limit: Einstein (1950) scaling; uniform grains.

geomorphology.name: diffusive_hillslope_flux
geomorphology.title: Linear diffusive sediment flux of soil creep
geomorphology.why: Creep moves soil downhill at a rate proportional to the slope, so convex hilltops lower and their profiles obey a diffusion equation.
geomorphology.limit: Gilbert (1909) and Culling (1960): gentle soil-mantled slopes; the flux grows faster than linearly near the angle of repose (see :func:`nonlinear_hillslope_flux`).

geomorphology.name: nonlinear_hillslope_flux
geomorphology.title: Nonlinear soil flux that diverges at a critical gradient
geomorphology.why: Steep slopes shed soil far faster than linear creep predicts, which is why hillslopes near their threshold angle become planar.
geomorphology.limit: Roering, Kirchner and Dietrich (1999): reduces to :func:`diffusive_hillslope_flux` on gentle slopes; landslides take over at the critical gradient.

geomorphology.name: scarp_elevation
geomorphology.title: Elevation across a fault scarp degraded by linear diffusion

params.name: distance
params.unit: m from the scarp midpoint, positive toward the upthrown side

params.name: half_offset
params.unit: m, half the vertical offset of the initial step

params.name: far_field_gradient
params.unit: 1, the regional slope on both sides

geomorphology.expr: half_offset * erf(distance / (2 * np.sqrt(diffusivity * time))) + far_field_gradient * distance
geomorphology.why: A fresh step in the land rounds off at a rate set by the hillslope diffusivity, so its shape records its age.
geomorphology.limit: Culling (1960) and Hanks et al. (1984): a vertical step on a uniform slope degraded by linear diffusion without base-level change; a fresh step (``diffusivity * time = 0``) is returned exactly.

geomorphology.name: scarp_maximum_gradient
geomorphology.title: Steepest gradient of a diffusively degraded fault scarp
geomorphology.why: The midpoint slope of a scarp falls as the inverse square root of its age, the measurement behind morphologic dating.
geomorphology.limit: Hanks et al. (1984), the derivative of :func:`scarp_elevation` at its midpoint; same assumptions.

geomorphology.name: soil_production_rate
geomorphology.title: Exponential soil production function

params.name: soil_depth
params.unit: m, vertical thickness of mobile soil

params.name: maximum_rate
params.unit: m/s of bedrock lowering under bare ground

geomorphology.why: Bedrock turns into soil fastest where it is bare and more slowly under a thick soil that shields it, which keeps soil-mantled hillslopes in balance.
geomorphology.limit: Heimsath et al. (1997), from cosmogenic nuclides under soils of a few metres at most; some sites show a humped function with a maximum under a thin soil.

geomorphology.name: hilltop_curvature
geomorphology.title: Hilltop curvature of a diffusive hillslope in steady state
geomorphology.why: Where creep balances uniform lowering, faster erosion makes sharper ridges, so the curvature of a hilltop measures its erosion rate.
geomorphology.limit: Roering, Perron and Kirchner (2007): steady state with linear creep at the divide, where the gradient is small.

geomorphology.name: stream_power_erosion
geomorphology.title: Bedrock incision rate of the stream-power law

params.name: drainage_area
params.unit: m^2, the area upstream, a proxy for discharge

params.name: erodibility
params.unit: m^(1 - 2 area_exponent)/s for a slope exponent of 1

geomorphology.why: A river cuts its bed faster where it carries more water down a steeper slope, the rule behind most models of mountain landscapes.
geomorphology.limit: Howard and Kerby (1983): detachment-limited bedrock channels, with discharge and width folded into powers of the area; no threshold, sediment cover or tools effect.

geomorphology.name: steady_state_slope
geomorphology.title: Channel slope at which stream-power incision balances uplift

params.name: erodibility
params.unit: m^(1 - 2 area_exponent)/s for a slope exponent of 1

geomorphology.why: A graded bedrock river steepens until it cuts down as fast as the rock rises, so its slope falls with drainage area along a concave profile.
geomorphology.limit: Steady state of :func:`stream_power_erosion` under uniform uplift; the slope follows Flint's law with concavity ``area_exponent / slope_exponent``.

geomorphology.name: knickpoint_celerity
geomorphology.title: Upstream migration speed of a knickpoint under stream power

params.name: slope
params.unit: 1, the channel slope at the knickpoint

params.name: erodibility
params.unit: m^(1 - 2 area_exponent)/s for a slope exponent of 1

geomorphology.why: A drop in base level travels up a river as a step that moves fastest on the large trunk streams and slows as it climbs into the headwaters.
geomorphology.limit: Whipple and Tucker (1999), the characteristic speed of :func:`stream_power_erosion`; independent of the slope only when ``slope_exponent = 1``, where knickpoints keep their shape.

geomorphology.name: flint_slope
geomorphology.title: Flint's power law of channel slope against drainage area
geomorphology.why: Along almost every river the slope falls as a power of the area drained, so a log-log plot of slope against area is a straight line whose slope is the concavity.
geomorphology.limit: Flint (1974): below the colluvial-fluvial transition at about 1 km^2, in rivers without knickpoints or changes of lithology.

geomorphology.name: chi_coordinate
geomorphology.title: The chi coordinate of a river long profile
geomorphology.expr: chi = integral of (reference_area / drainage_area)**concavity d distance
geomorphology.why: Rescaling distance by drainage area turns a graded profile into a straight line, so tributaries that share a base level and erosion rate plot on top of each other.
geomorphology.limit: Perron and Royden (2013), integrated by the trapezoidal rule between nodes; in steady state with :func:`steady_state_slope` the elevation is linear in chi.

geomorphology.name: hack_length
geomorphology.title: Hack's law of main-stream length against drainage area

params.name: coefficient
params.unit: m^(1 - 2 exponent), about 0.32 for an exponent of 0.6 in SI (1.4 in miles)

geomorphology.why: Larger basins are longer than they are wide, because the main stream grows faster than the square root of the area it drains.
geomorphology.limit: Hack (1957), from basins in Virginia and Maryland; the exponent drifts toward 0.5 in the largest basins.

geomorphology.name: strahler_order
geomorphology.title: Strahler order of every link in a river network

params.name: downstream
params.unit: Index of the link each link drains into, -1 at an outlet

geomorphology.expr: order = max(upstream orders) + (count of that maximum >= 2)
geomorphology.why: Ordering streams from the headwaters down, rising by one only where two streams of equal order meet, gives the network a hierarchy whose counts and lengths follow Horton's laws.
geomorphology.limit: Strahler (1952, 1957): a link takes the highest order among those draining into it, plus one when two or more share that highest order; several outlets are allowed.

geomorphology.name: downstream_hydraulic_geometry
geomorphology.title: Width, depth and velocity of a channel as powers of discharge

params.name: discharge
params.unit: m^3/s, the bankfull or mean discharge

geomorphology.expr: width = a * Q**b; depth = c * Q**f; velocity = Q / (width * depth)
geomorphology.why: Rivers adjust their shape to the water they carry, widening fastest, deepening more slowly and speeding up least.
geomorphology.limit: Leopold and Maddock (1953): power laws fitted to gauging stations, with the velocity from continuity so that its coefficient and exponent are ``1 / (a c)`` and ``1 - b - f``.
geomorphology.output_unit: width m; depth m; velocity m/s

geomorphology.name: effective_discharge
geomorphology.title: Effective discharge that carries the most sediment over time

params.name: log_standard_deviation
params.unit: 1, standard deviation of the natural logarithm of discharge

params.name: rating_exponent
params.unit: 1, ``b`` in the sediment rating ``Qs = a Q**b``, usually 1.5-3

geomorphology.why: Rare floods move the most sediment per event but ordinary flows happen far more often; their product peaks at a moderate, frequent flood that does most of the geomorphic work.
geomorphology.limit: Wolman and Miller (1960), with a lognormal frequency of discharge and a power-law sediment rating; the maximum of ``Q**b`` times the lognormal density.

geomorphology.name: threshold_shear_velocity
geomorphology.title: Fluid threshold shear velocity for wind to lift sand

params.name: coefficient
params.unit: 1, about 0.1 for the fluid threshold and 0.08 for the lower impact threshold

geomorphology.expr: coefficient * np.sqrt((sediment_density - air_density) / air_density * gravity * diameter)
geomorphology.why: Wind starts to move sand once the drag on a grain overcomes its weight, which takes a stronger wind for coarser grains.
geomorphology.limit: Bagnold (1941): dry cohesionless sand coarser than about 0.1 mm; moisture, crusts and fine grains raise the threshold.

geomorphology.name: bagnold_sand_flux
geomorphology.title: Bagnold's saltation mass flux of blown sand

params.name: coefficient
params.unit: 1, 1.5 for uniform, 1.8 for naturally graded and 2.8 for poorly sorted sand

geomorphology.why: The mass of sand carried by the wind grows as the cube of the shear velocity, so a few storms move most of a desert's sand.
geomorphology.limit: Bagnold (1941), referred to a 0.25 mm sand; well above the threshold, since it has no threshold term (see :func:`kawamura_sand_flux`).

geomorphology.name: kawamura_sand_flux
geomorphology.title: Kawamura's saltation mass flux with a threshold
geomorphology.expr: coefficient * air_density / gravity * np.maximum(u - ut, 0) * (u + ut)**2; u = shear_velocity; ut = threshold_shear_velocity
geomorphology.why: Below the threshold the wind moves no sand at all, and just above it only a little, which Bagnold's cube law misses.
geomorphology.limit: Kawamura (1951): steady saltation over a flat dry sand bed; tends to the cube law far above the threshold.

geomorphology.name: dune_migration_rate
geomorphology.title: Migration rate of a dune that keeps its shape

params.name: bulk_density
params.unit: kg/m^3 of the deposited sand, about 1600

geomorphology.why: Sand blown over the crest settles on the lee face, so a dune advances by the sand flux divided by its height; small dunes outrun large ones.
geomorphology.limit: Bagnold (1941): a two-dimensional dune of constant shape that traps all the sand crossing its crest.

geomorphology.name: cosmogenic_production_at_depth
geomorphology.title: Cosmogenic-nuclide production rate beneath the surface
geomorphology.why: Cosmic-ray neutrons are absorbed within the top two metres of rock, so a grain begins to accumulate nuclides only as erosion brings it close to the surface.
geomorphology.limit: Lal (1991): neutron spallation only, on a flat surface; muons dominate below a few metres.

geomorphology.name: cosmogenic_concentration
geomorphology.title: Concentration of a cosmogenic nuclide in an eroding surface

params.name: time
params.unit: s of exposure, starting from zero concentration

geomorphology.expr: production_rate / r * (1 - np.exp(-r * time)); r = decay_constant + density * erosion_rate / attenuation_length
geomorphology.why: Nuclides build up until decay and erosion remove them as fast as cosmic rays make them, so a surface's concentration records either its exposure age or its erosion rate.
geomorphology.limit: Lal (1991): steady erosion and production, spallation only, no inheritance; ``production_rate * time`` when neither decay nor erosion removes nuclides.

geomorphology.name: steady_state_erosion_rate
geomorphology.title: Erosion rate from a steady-state cosmogenic-nuclide concentration
geomorphology.why: A surface that has eroded steadily for long enough carries a concentration inversely proportional to its erosion rate, the basis of catchment-wide denudation rates from river sand.
geomorphology.limit: Lal (1991), the inverse of :func:`cosmogenic_concentration` at long times; valid once the surface has been exposed for several times ``attenuation_length / (density * erosion_rate)``.

geomorphology.name: morphologic_age
geomorphology.title: Morphologic age of a fault scarp from its steepest gradient
geomorphology.why: Measuring a scarp's height and steepest slope gives the product of diffusivity and age, which dates the earthquake once the diffusivity is calibrated.
geomorphology.limit: Hanks et al. (1984), inverting :func:`scarp_maximum_gradient`: one rupture, linear diffusion and no base-level change at the foot.

geomorphology.name: luminescence_age
geomorphology.title: Luminescence burial age of a sediment

params.name: equivalent_dose
params.unit: Gy, the laboratory dose that reproduces the natural signal

params.name: dose_rate
params.unit: Gy/s from the surrounding sediment and cosmic rays

geomorphology.why: Quartz and feldspar grains store the radiation dose received since sunlight last emptied their traps, which dates when a dune or flood deposit was buried.
geomorphology.limit: Aitken (1985): complete bleaching at deposition, a constant dose rate and no fading or saturation of the signal.
